review:
Psycho Starship Rampage, developed by Ballistic Frogs and published by TyGAMES, is an inventive blend of roguelite structure and arcade-style shoot ’em up action that distinguishes itself through an unusually deep and flexible ship-building system. While it initially presents itself as a fast-paced side-scrolling shooter, it quickly becomes clear that its true focus lies in experimentation and customization, encouraging players to construct and refine their own spacecraft rather than simply pilot a predefined one.

The game places players in control of an AI-driven warship navigating hostile sectors of space, with the overarching goal of rebuilding itself through scavenged components. Each run follows a familiar roguelite loop: progress through procedurally generated encounters, defeat enemies, collect resources, and use those resources to expand and improve your ship. This structure ensures that no two runs feel exactly the same, as the combination of available upgrades and encountered challenges constantly shifts. However, the real depth of the experience comes not from the progression system itself, but from how players choose to build and adapt their ship during each attempt.

Ship construction is the defining feature of Psycho Starship Rampage. Instead of selecting upgrades from a simple menu, players physically assemble their vessel using modular components that can be attached in nearly any configuration. Weapons, engines, power generators, and defensive modules all occupy space on a grid, and their placement directly affects performance, balance, and survivability. This system allows for a remarkable degree of creativity, enabling players to design anything from compact, maneuverable ships to sprawling, heavily armed constructs. The interplay between different components adds a layer of strategy, as players must consider not only what to equip but also how to arrange it effectively.

Combat builds on this customization, offering fast-paced, chaotic encounters that reward both reflexes and planning. The game follows a horizontal shoot ’em up format, with players navigating through waves of enemies and environmental hazards while unleashing their chosen arsenal. The variety of weapons and possible configurations means that each build can feel distinct, whether focusing on overwhelming firepower, defensive resilience, or unconventional tactics. However, while the customization system is rich and engaging, the core combat mechanics can feel comparatively straightforward, with enemy patterns and encounter structures that may become repetitive over extended play.

The roguelite elements add both replayability and unpredictability, but they also introduce some inconsistency. Progression is tied to unlocking new components and gradually improving available options, which encourages repeated runs. At the same time, the randomness of each playthrough can lead to uneven experiences, where some runs provide powerful combinations while others leave players struggling with limited resources. This variability can be exciting, but it can also feel frustrating, particularly when difficulty spikes occur without clear warning.

Visually, the game adopts a retro-inspired aesthetic that emphasizes clarity and movement. Ships are outlined with glowing elements, and the action is presented in a way that prioritizes readability during intense moments. The overall style is functional rather than detailed, but it suits the fast-paced nature of the gameplay. The soundtrack complements this approach with energetic, electronic tracks that maintain momentum and reinforce the sense of constant motion.

An additional layer of interest comes from the cooperative mode, which allows multiple players to control different aspects of the same ship. This feature introduces a unique dynamic, as players must coordinate their actions while managing a shared structure. It can lead to chaotic and entertaining moments, especially when communication breaks down or when the ship itself becomes unwieldy due to excessive modifications. While not the central focus of the game, it adds variety and offers an alternative way to engage with its mechanics.

Despite its strengths, Psycho Starship Rampage does have some rough edges. The learning curve can be steep, particularly when it comes to understanding the interactions between different components and optimizing ship designs. The interface, while serviceable, can feel slightly cumbersome when managing larger builds, and the balance between customization and combat is not always consistent. Over time, the repetition of enemy encounters and the limited evolution of gameplay mechanics can also reduce the sense of progression.

Ultimately, the game stands out for its ambition and creativity. It takes the familiar structure of a shoot ’em up and transforms it into a sandbox for experimentation, where the process of building and refining a ship becomes as important as the action itself. While it may not achieve perfect balance in every aspect, it offers a distinctive experience that rewards curiosity and adaptability.

Rating: 8/10

This game isn't a disaster, but it just isn't really finished from a design standpoint. It has about 80% of what it would need to be a great game, but as it stands it's little more than a proof of concept for its ship-construction mechanic. The stage, enemy, and rogue/RNG aspects of the game need a complete and total overhaul for it to work well. It's worth looking at on a deep sale to see the concepts at play, but don't expect to get much fun or satisfaction out of it past the first couple of hours, at which point you will have seen all it has to offer. The dev is clearly a competent programmer, this game just needed more time and perhaps some different voices to reach its full potential; I don't know why it was left in this state, whether because they felt no further desire to work on it, thought it was complete, or simply ran out of resources to continue, but I hope they work on future projects and that those projects are better and more successful than this one.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

[h1]The most frustrating game I have ever played.[/h1]


It's not the hardest, nor is it the worst, far from it. But it is the game that has brought me the most pain, specifically because it has such potential but squanders it.

Psycho Starship Rampage has a visually striking asthetic reminiscent of vector based graphics like the Vectrex and the ship-building part is fantastic. You can customize your ship with a variety of different parts and really make it yours. Do you want a small and nimble rocket that drops mines while avoiding enemies? You can build that. Do you prefer a gigantic Star Destroyer with loads of lasers and shields to power through enemy waves? That's also possible. A big cube of death that rams into enemies and crush bosses with its sheer weight? Go wild! Essentially any type of ship you can dream up, you can build.

But all this potential is wasted when you get into the actual game. It starts off fine, fun even! But as you keep playing It gets difficult in unfair and frustrating ways, and questionable design decisions sour what could have been a hidden gem.

My issues can be summed up as follows:

• Perma-death: In itself not necessarely a bad thing, many games have used perma-death in the past in ways that created tension and rewarded skill. But for a game to implement perma-death it needs to be fair to the player and avoid things like instant death traps which can lead to hours of progress lost in an instant without much warning, if any at all.
Speaking of...

• Insta-death: Psycho Starship Rampage has several instant or near instant kill mechanics which can ruin a run in the blink of an eye, many of which are unavoidable if you're unlucky. First of there's laser-type enemies. Yes, lasers are cool when you use them but giving them to the enemies is rather bold.

Not only do they cover the entire screen instantly making dodging them nearly impossible, but some enemies lock on making it actually impossible to dodge. They can also hide behind other enemies and asteroids while firing meaning you can't even reach them and attempt to destroy them before they fire.
There's no warning when they appear either, despite their extreme threat level. I'd say the laser enemies are more dangerous than most bosses, yet you don't get even a hint of a warning that they're there until it's too late. You need to keep your eyes peeled for them at all times which is difficult to do when the screen is filled with obstacles and other enemies. Even if you do spot them, good luck taking them out before they do the same to you. Now in the game's defense there are a few laser enemies that are done right. They move in a predictable way and only fire their laser in short spurts allowing you to move past them when the laser is down, but these are in the minority.

Then there are laser-type bosses which also kill you instantly and seem to be balanced around the player moving behind asteroids to hide from their beam, but sometimes asteroids don't spawn in. If your ship is fast enough you can sometimes outrun the laser, but some bosses lock on with their laser making this impossible.
There are also asteroids which often take up nearly the entire screen making it impossible to avoid them unless you have strong enough weapons and/or blend into the background making them difficult to see.

I do actually fancy myself pretty good at shoot-em'-ups and bullet hell games. I've beaten the majority of the Touhou franchise on Lunatic and CAVE's notoriously difficult Deathsmiles on the hardest difficulty setting. The difference between those games and Psycho Starship Rampage is that in those games the player is equipped to deal with the insane difficulty in various ways, be it a small hitbox or bombs that instantly clear the screen. Movement is precise and snappy and stages are always the same both in terms of enemy placement and bullet pattern, allowing the player to memorize them and improve with each run.
Here, such is not the case...

• Imprecise controls and unfair mechanics: In this game your movement is anything but precise. Your ship floats around as if on ice, which could work in a slower paced shooter where you want to emphasize the effect (or lack there of) which outer space has on a spaceships traversal.

But this is a fast-paced action games like the arcade shooters of old, and this type of movement does not mesh well with the rest of the game's design. You also do not have invurnerability frames when getting hit like in most arcade games, or a small hitbox to let you avoid damage to begin with like in bullet hell games with similar amounts of obstacles, instead your entire ship is a weakspot.

This could have been an interesting trade off where smaller ships are more maneuverable and safer to pilot but weaker against bosses, while bigger ships are riskier but can dish out more damage. It does start of that way but because of how enemy scaling works in this game, combined with how they leave behind wrecks when destroyed means you cannot afford to build a low-firepower ship or you will be swarmed and overrun.
All this paired with the fact that you do not have extra lives like in old-school arcade games, or meaningful powerups to help you makes for a very awkward and unfair difficulty curve with huge spikes owing to my next point...

Randomness: The game is full of it, and in my opinion it is perhaps its biggest flaw. I believe the developer's intent was to make the game more replayable with different outcomes each run, but it has some very harsh consequences which drag the entire game down and often leads to situations you cannot overcome regardless of player skill.

First of all, stages are random. There's no way to memorize enemy layouts or bullet patterns and you might get stages full of insta-kill laser enemies or be blessed with a stage void of them. Enemy drops which you can use to build your ship are also random. You might get a really good shield early on, or you might go an entire run without seeing one. You might get nothing but repairbots and generators, meaning your offensive capablities are so low you will get overrun by enemies.

All this means potential progress essentially comes down to luck. Luck in terms of getting good enough equipment to stat-check the enemies, and in not having the game spawn laser enemies or bosses. If you get lucky enough you can breeze through the game with minimal effort. If lady luck is not on your side however, you'll be in for a very rough time.

I wish the game toned down the use of laser enemies, or at least gave them a drawback like less damage to make up for their instant, screen-range coverage or a cooldown, that'd be a good start. If the game either reduced randomness or at least gave you more options from drops making you less reliant on luck to get a decent ship that would be another improvement.

I might be looking at this game from the wrong perspective in that I see it as a bullet-hell game with awkward movement and a hitbox covering your entire ship, but I think the game needs to give players more options for dealing with the onslaught of enemies and obstacles to make it a more fair and enjoyable experience. It feels like it's taking influence from both old arcade space shooters and more modern bullet-hell shooters, but it doesn't stick the landing because of the way they were combined. Add in the perma-death and randomness and you're left with a right mess...

It really is a shame because with some changes this game could be something truly special. But because of how it views difficulty and how it treats the player's time, I cannot recommend it.
So much unrealized potential. Don't bother unless it's ultra cheap.

Psycho Starship Rampage scratched an itch that I didn't know that I had.  It's been a lot of fun in the short time I've played it.  The downside to the game is that play sessions can last a lot longer than you anticipated as you go "just one more round" round after round.  The basic premise of an FTL-style map and progression combined with shoot-em-up gameplay is engaging enough, and the learning curve is just enough that you feel satisfied when you get over it.

I finished the campaign on my second try.  The basic strat of "get lots of scrap and don't die" works pretty well, and then you're down to your rolls on gear.  The ending felt pretty satisfying even if the end boss was anticlimactic by that point.

Despite all the fun, there were parts of the game that were annoying:  Space terrain (floating rocks) is heavily RNG: sometimes your screen will be full of enormous boulders with no way around. The space rocks aren't very obvious as well, and fail to stand out when the screen is full of bullets going every-which-way.  Enemies rubber-band hard when knocked off their path, and will happily careen through rocks and the player ship to get where they're going.  Even bosses: if your boss fight is full of space rocks, they're a much larger threat than the boss itself due to how much the bosses send them flying around.  I've also had a few times where I've gotten boxed into a corner by a boss who would proceed to bonk against me until it exploded because my hull had more HP; not a very satisfying way to win a boss fight.

Edit 07/18/2023: Survival mode, on the other hand, seems kinda rubbish.  It ought to be fun, but the above-mentioned gameplay issues along with no repairs outside the repair drops mean you get to play a game of "sell damaged stuff and buy the exact same stuff new."  This is the opposite of fun gameplay.  "You unlock stuff when you die!" Punishing players for surviving (in a survival mode) is also not fun gameplay.  The alleged "leaderboard" that attempted to load after I died still had not loaded after ten minutes of waiting, and even if it did would the score compare the death 0 run to everyone else's heavily-rng-dependent death-0 run, or to every run?  To improve this mode, unlocks should activate upon achievement, not death. If you want to include a no-unlocks challenge, then make that a toggle and a separate leaderboard. Include "Repair all" to remove the annoying "sell and re-buy everything" gameplay. Suddenly you have a fun, relatively-balanced, and rewarding survival mode.

In Summary, Psycho Starship Rampage is a lot of fun.  Don't expect AAA-quality, just blast stuff, collect scrap, buy upgrades and that's all you need.  Play the campaign until you win, or play survival while you're bad so you can collect deaths, otherwise you'll be punished by un-fun gameplay.  I did enjoy it and felt the money well-spent, but after that survival I'm done.

If you have the nerves of steel, the patience of a saint and the abundant free time of an unemployed person then this is the perfect game for you. If you are like most of the mere mortals then this is just an unbalanced time-wasting mess of a game that is designed to screw your progress by any (unfair) means possible and mock you further after wrecking your nerves.

Ship customization is the best part of the game but it also has its flaws (unable to see TOTAL HP, power output & usage & storage, DPS of your ship as a whole). But, it just feels awful when I lose hours of meticulous customizations and upgrades in a matter of seconds.  

Achievements are tricky, grindy and dumb -- apparently dying over and over is an achievement, which is very easy to "accomplish" in Survival mode. I played the campaign for over 7 hours and none of the achievements were unlocked. Then I started playing the Survival mode as suggested by a fellow gamer on the forums and the achievements finally started unlocking. I even got the friendly-fire achievements in [b]Survival mode's hyperspace (out of the combat)[/b] by crashing into my own mines. WTF?!

So the Campaign mode doesn't unlock achievements or new abilities and unlocking abilities in Survival mode doesn't affect the Campaign. Seems like the Campaign mode was an afterthought; an orphan that didn't get the love it deserved.

Also saving your progress manually during the campaign means nothing to this game. You won't be able to continue from your manual save if/when you (inevitably) experience perma-death and you'll have to start from scratch again.

Numerous enemies and humongous asteroids will squeeze you into a tiny space you can (not) move. Also enemies will rush/ram into your ship from all 4 sides on the 2D plane and from any angle without any indication whatsoever. Huge bosses will run circles around you and do acrobatics while you can't do a slight rotation or spin. As the boss gets more enraged it moves and fires faster, increasing its DPS. I had so many loooong boss fights (some around 5 minutes long but felt like an eternity) where my ship was destroyed by stuff I didn't see, or the boss just decided to ram into my ship when I successfully evaded its fire. I had also many short boss fights where my ship was either immobilized or insta-killed by a single-shot of tracking laser.

Apparently, it is more important for me to see the Rage level of the boss rather than its remaining HP. The gargantuan boss rage bar and the other UI elements also hide grave dangers such as asteroids or boss fire from your view. I would have preferred the UI elements to be much smaller and at least their backgrounds to be transparent. An option to hide the boss rage bar, etc. and display its HP instead would have been welcome.

It has taken me a ot longer to get to the point where I felt I could write a review on this one. Mostly because they leave a lot of the learning up to you, and experimentation. That's not my favorite thing, but the game has enough going for it that I can over look that.
It is a game that would benefit from a good guide however. 
The core concept here is that the player is an insane war machine trying to get home, and destroying all of the apparently innocent people between it and Earth.
As you progress, you pick up scrap and new tech and build yourself up into a better and better ship. 
It is in the building that the games explanation is lacking. I really don't get a sense that I know what anything but the guns really do. Obviously the engines more you, but I don't feel a difference between one level one and four level four engines. And what is the difference between the lightning bolts and the batteries? I feel like they should have something to do with how long my guns can shoot, but the connection is tenuous at best.
That said, I have had fun playing with it, and trying to understand it better. If you consider that part of the game, it is a good one. 
A quick tip, you can test your guns in hyperspace, very useful as it is possible to build guns in such a way that some don't seem to fire, and when plasma bolts hit each other they seem to adjust the trajectory, so it is important to make sure that if you are doing any kind of wide spread you check for clear lines of fire. 
Other than that, not much to say. Straight left to right scroller. You zip around killing ships, collecting scrap and a shall handful of other things that drop, fighting was after wave of ships, before tackling a boss. 
There seems to be a pretty wide variety of ship types, and their tactics. 
It isn't easy, but it does seem fun. 
An easy thumbs up.
ADDENDUM: 58 hours start to finish of the campaign. All of the achievement however are in survival, so I earned none of them. Still, great fun. The ships can be so different depending on what you find I will probably play it a few more times before putting it away. Good game.

[i][b]Aux commandes d'un vaisseau intelligent, votre but est de tuer tout le monde. Chaque survivant représente une perte de ressources pour votre prochaine évolution. Face aux armées qui remplirons votre écran, il faudra compter sur vos réflexes, mais aussi sur l'efficacité du vaisseau que vous allez vous-même concevoir.[/b][/i]

[h1]Des voix dans ma tête.[/h1]

Vous êtes donc une intelligence artificielle, récemment éveillée et plongée dans une folie meurtrière. Vous êtes capable de rapidement démonter votre vaisseau pour le remonter comme bon vous semble entre deux combats. Votre seule faille, c'est le siège de votre intelligence, qui tient dans un carré de 4 cases. Cette partie de votre vaisseau ne pourra jamais bouger et si elle vient à être détruite, c'est la mort.

[h1]Mes armes sont chargées et tout est magnifique.[/h1]

Pour protéger le cœur, on place des blocs tout autours du vaisseau. Plus un bloc est gros et plus il est difficile à détruire pour les ennemis, mais plus il coûte de débris. Bien entendu, votre but étant de massacrer vos ennemis et non pas juste de résister à leurs coups, il va aussi falloir monter des modules sur vos blocs de métal : Des canons, des batteries, des générateurs, etc. On commence la partie avec un vaisseau déjà monté, mais ce sera à vous de le faire évoluer pour l'adapter et le faire évoluer au fur et à mesure que vous récolterez débris et nouvelles technologies.

[h1]J'aime l'odeur du plasma de bon matin.[/h1]

Une fois votre vaisseau passé en revue, il est temps de combattre. Les ennemis tirent des projectiles qu'il faudra chercher à éviter, mais votre vaisseau peut soutenir quelques coups et vous possédez un puissant module de réparation automatique, régénérant rapidement vos parties endommagées. Néanmoins, lorsque l'un de vos blocs est trop fortement touché, il ne protège plus les blocs de derrière, laissant potentiellement des modules sensibles à découvert. Si vos armes sont endommagées, elles ne tirent plus. Si votre moteur est cassé, vous ne pourrez plus esquiver et si votre cœur est brisé, c'est la mort. Votre vaisseau est donc capable sans broncher de subir quelques dégâts de temps en temps, mais trop dégâts sur une courte période peuvent complètement détruire vos systèmes.

[h1]Il y a un trou. Dans mon esprit.[/h1]

Créer un vaisseau solide n'est pas évident. Il faut bien sur tenter de minimiser la taille pour mieux esquiver les projectiles. Chaque dégât encaissé coûte du métal à réparer, donc moins vous en subissez, mieux c'est. Mais le plus sûr est souvent d'avoir des éléments de coque vide tout autour de votre vaisseau pour encaisser les dégâts. Il faut aussi bien réfléchir aux modules les plus exposés. Si vos armes sont à l'avant du vaisseau, il y a fort à parier qu'elles seront détruites en premier, vous laissant sans défenses et il est préférable de toujours garder au moins quelques générateurs bien protégés pour avoir quelques ressources même en cas de dégâts critique. La disposition de votre vaisseau est une étape importante qui nécessite beaucoup d'adaptation en fonction des modules et du nombre de débris disponibles.

[h1]Je vous informe de mon usage actuel d'armes létales.[/h1]

Employer une arme coûte de l'énergie et il faudra souvent faire des pauses entre deux tirs pour qu'elles puissent se recharger.  Il existe une grande variété d'armes, chacune possédant ses propres forces ou faiblesses. Le rayon tracteur nécessite d'avoir des astéroïdes sous la main mais cause des dégâts énormes, le bélier est puissant mais coûte cher en énergie et est dur à employer, le rayon laser consomme votre énergie en quelques secondes mais cause des dégâts énormes, le générateur de mine ou de trous noirs possèdent un temps de rechargement long, etc. Tout est utilisable et la meilleur solution dépend surtout des options que le hasard vous laisse.

[h1]3418eme guerre interstellaire.[/h1]

Deux modes de jeux sont proposés, le mode campagne reprend une carte de l'univers façon FTL, avec une flotte qui vous poursuit, bloquant peu à peu la partie la plus simple de la carte et vous contraignant à naviguer vers les secteurs difficiles. La terre et ses alentours sont puissamment défendus, il faudra prendre votre temps pour parcourir l'univers, juste devant la flotte, et récupérer un maximum d'éléments pour améliorer votre vaisseau. Si les secteurs deviennent trop difficile pour vous, vous finirez par rater des cibles, des débris, des technologies, augmenter vos difficultés pour le niveau suivant, et finalement mourir. Éviter de tomber dans une mauvaise dynamique requiert une stratégie méticuleuse.

[h1] Survivre. Détruire. Évoluer.[/h1]

Pour le mode survie, pas le droit à l'échec, la moindre faute vous fera directement recommencer à la case départ et il n'y a pas d’objectifs finaux à atteindre, si ce n'est les succès qui pourrons être collectés. En comparaison, le mode survie se concentre plus sur la compétence du joueur, la personnalisation possible du vaisseau y est bien moindre, vous ne commencerez d'ailleurs qu'avec des technologies très basiques et les autres se débloqueront avec les succès. Il faudra souvent se contenter de peu et compter uniquement sur vos réflexes. Le mode campagne propose un scénario minimal et une dimension stratégique supplémentaire, mais ne donne aucun succès, qui plus est les parties étant plus longue, la mort y est d'autant plus frustrante.

[h1]Je suis l'Apex de la création.[/h1]

La musique est énergique et engageante, très synthétique (ce qui colle plutôt bien au côté SF) et avec un rythme fort (bien adapté aux combats). Les quelques voix rajoutent à l'ambiance et le feedback sonore est dans l'ensemble très bon.
Les graphismes sont jolis mais posent parfois quelques problèmes de lisibilité, lorsqu'un ennemi passe sur une nébuleuse, ou pire encore quand il y a des roches à esquiver dans un champs d’astéroïdes : Il est aisé de confondre les petits rochers avec le fond visuel, or les astéroïdes sont souvent plus dangereux que les ennemis eux-mêmes, dans lesquels on rentre régulièrement de façon volontaire pour éviter qu'ils ne s'échappent. Le bon côté des choses, c'est que les ennemis subissent aussi les rochers et on voit régulièrement des boss s'empaler contre un gros rocher, se suicidant littéralement sans affrontement.
On regrettera aussi l'absence de modes multijoueurs. Le jeu semble offrir la possibilité de jouer jusqu'à 4 en local, mais sans offrir le moindre mode de jeu adaptés. Probablement des restes d'idées jamais implémentées.

[h1]Ils sont morts. Les voix se taisent, pour l'instant.[/h1]

PSR possède une rejouabilité considérable, dûe à la richesse de la création de vaisseau, dans le choix des armes et de tout ce qui va autour, avec des modificateurs aléatoires qui peuvent parfois drastiquement changer l'utilité de chaque module. Un bouclier peut par exemple arrêter les projectiles énergétiques, ralentir ce qui passe dans son champs, dévier les tirs dans une zone d'effet bien plus grande, etc. Autant de choses qui permettront de voir les combats sous un angle différent.

PSR parvient à bien mixer différents éléments. Jeu de tir nerveux et difficile bien que rarement immédiatement punitif, la création du vaisseau apporte réellement un élément de réflexion intéressant et les deux éléments sont entremêlés de belle manière, il faudra parvenir à maîtriser les deux aspects du jeu pour aller loin.

If you enjoyed Tyrian 2000 from way back in the day, you're likely to love this game, as it plays fairly similar in both in game play and the ability to customize your ship to your liking (though this one is more intricate).  I loved being able to design my ship from individual parts, it allowed for a massive degree of customization, and the fact that I could sell back parts at full value meant I never felt afraid to try new things because I knew I could always undo them if they didn't work out.

While the random drops of equipment can be kind of annoying, I found later that I actually liked it, because it can force you to make interesting choices.  All your plasma cannon drops lately have sucked, so do you deal with a massive ship of weak but high quality weapons, a small but overpriced ship of powerful but relatively low quality weapons, or switch to other weapon types entirely that you're less comfortable with?

I actually found myself using exceedingly old weapons at one point because it had a rare quality that let it be fit on the smallest ship parts, so even though it was a bit expensive and weak, my ship was absolutely tiny because of it.

The difficulty seemed about right, though I found some of the latter levels too easy, and I hadn't even spent time harvesting some of the prior levels for additional scrap like I could have ahead of the time limit.  I did however die a few times along the way, so it isn't as though it was entirely too easy.

This game is everything I was asking for when I bought it, and I love it.

Gameplay sessions are fairly short, as it is a roguelike.  The ship creation is just in-depth enough to keep one's attention, keep one experimenting, and allow for a favored style of play, and, at the same time, it's not so complex that it's confusing.  Personally, I'd like to see them add, if anything, more complex control options, since they force you to consider different, more specific key bindings.  I think that's a phenomenal system.

39 hours in, and not only do I still have a bit to unlock, but I'm experimenting with builds like some sort of digital tinker, or a scripter or something.  

One thing to expect:  since your ship can change completely from stage to stage, and because you'll pick up random new modules (Diablo-esque items), your ship probably WILL change drastically every couple of stages.  It helps keep things fresh, but means that you'll also need to put in a little more time and dedication for successful runs, since your 'ideal ship' won't last for more than a few stages.  This is a bit of a numbers game, in that regard.

All in all:  Yes.  Just, this whole thing: Yes.

"Just one more level and I can upgrade this subsystem..."

It's one of those games. You know which ones I'm talking about. "Just 5 more minutes..." turn into "Why are the birds so loud this late? Oh...". 

So, what is the game about? 

Basically it's a 2D arcade-style side-scrolling shooter with 2 game modes (campaign&survival). What sets it apart from the generic shooter, apart from being quite polished and having rock solid gameplay&controls, is the upgrade/weapon handling. Between each level you are able to modify your ship more or less from scratch. Layout, engine, energy generators, energy storage, weapons, defensive systems and lots of other addons like tractor beams or loot magnets are at your disposal. And that's about it. 

What makes it work is how well it comes together. The gameplay itself is solid (if somewhat repetetive), the levels are just about the right length not to get boring, the upgrade system offers lots of stuff to play with but is really straightforward and easy to use. 

That said, there is room for improvement. The variety of enemies is fairly small, the level design is rather basic and while gamepads are supported there is no option to configure it properly (some buttons can be mapped ingame but that doesn't help much). As steam offers a controller remapping it's not a big issue but an ingame configuration would be nice.

Overall I think this is a really enjoyable, above-average shooter with decent replayability. I wouldn't necessarily recommend it to hardcore bullet hell fans (if I can beat it casually it's probaly too easy ;) ) but to anyone who enjoys a decent arcade shooter with lots of customization options. Would definitely buy it again.

One thing that isn't rogue-like at least in the campaign is like FTL there are enemy ships homing for you on the main map so if you keep jumping and making progress you'll stay ahead of them, and if you die you get a few extra lives as each time you die the ships move one system closer to you.  Which is pretty great because sometimes you'll get boxed in and melt like plastic.

TL:DR - Geometry Wars and FTL made sweet sweet spaceship shooter love and birthed this gem!

I've played Gradius, R-Type, Ikaruga, RayForce, Touhou and on and on since I was a child. I'm not new to the genre. At all.
I'm using a controller, and PSR STILL feels like you're an ice cube sliding across a floor also covered in ice, shooting at snowflakes. Difficulty spikes and dips violently - it's either a little too easy or murderously hard (and I've tried several different routes with different difficulties). Blueprints are too random, so you're either OP early on or totally underpowered for the majority of a run.
There's a way to die without a run immediately ending, and revert to the previous system you were in to choose a different route, but I have no idea how this is triggered and there's no indication of how to earn 'lives' nor is there a counter of any kind. It happened to me once, and I was totally lost as to how it happened.

Some blueprints are way, way, way too expensive (I've never even seen what the black hole generator looks like, despite being frugal on scrap expenditure) and once you clear the campaign, your save just loads back to the mission before the end - so that masterpiece you've spent all that time building up and tinkering with basically gets shelved.
That's no fun at all.

It's an awesome concept. I feel like there was a lot left to experience, but the reward is not commensurate with the investment.
The campaign ending is brief but has a shocking and dark twist, hinting at a much deeper universe than we're shown...but there are no achievements or unlocks or anything for clearing it. At all. You would think there would be a NG+ system or something, or maybe a sandbox where you could test wacky builds, but no.

I can only hope some of this stuff comes as DLC. I know I would actually pay for it. For what it is, though, I recommend it just for the Saberhagen-esque experience.

Just finished the game and well, it kind of left me in a 50/50 feeling. I'll go to the good things first.

The ship customization is ingenious! It gives you all the freedom to create a ship that suits exactly your taste. This includes the shape, weapons, weapon directions, energytanks and so on. You can even assign different keybinds to different parts of the ship. It is easily the best part of the game.

Also destroying enemies feels great and satisfying. The music fits in the game quite well, though I only liked maybe one song. The songs resemble those annoying chiptune songs too much, but that's just my opinion, I don't count it as a flaw in the game. Graphics are also nice and flashy, kind of what you would expect from a space shooter.

While the ship customization is fantastic, along with some smaller things, the rest of the game isn't that tempting.

Starting with permadeath. Yeah you read it right, this game has permadeath, which affects many other things that ultimately lead to an unsatisfying gaming experience. Permadeath happens if the enemy wave reaches your position on the world (star) map. This means that you have about 6 lives, as every time you die, the wave moves closer to your position. This means no free exploring and collecting various items on the map, that you would maybe want.

You have to keep moving forward towards your goal. But you cannot move towards it too fast, since the levels are too hard compared to your level, so you always have to take the "easy", "medium" or at maximum the "hard" route. This means that you have to zigzag your way through the map. This then leads to a situation where you are only a couple of steps ahead of the permadeath wave at all times (so maybe 2 lives).

This then affects to your decisions regarding what weapons you'd like to equip. When you've found something that works, you cannot really differ from it, since if you try out a new setup and it doesn't work, you're back to your previous setup with maybe one life remaining. So there goes all the fun of trying out new things. Also you don't get to keep the items and scrap you collected before you died, which means no extra boost after death.

The enemies and levels are all the same, with the exception of enemy movement and bullet patterns. Every enemy and boss is the exact same red wireframe thing. Bosses have some kind of pattern, but mostly they just shoot masses of bullets everywhere. And yeah, don't expect any difference in the last level or boss either. Playing the levels just get boring halfway into the game. And the ship's acceleration and deceleration are more annoying than good game desing, though it does help with small movements, but I'd rather have none or very tiny values on those.

It's a damn shame, because the ship customization is so well done here, but the negative things really outweigh the positive. It's just annoying and frustrating most of the time to play this game. There is really nothing memorable outside the ship customization system. But this gives potential for future releases, I have to give it that. A slight thumbs down from me.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- Ship customization (10/10)
- Graphics (8/10)
- Loot system (9/10)

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Permadeath (1/10)
- Level variety (2/10)
- Enemy & boss variety (2/10)
- Difficulty curve & forgiveness (3/10)

[b]Final Score: (5/10)[/b]

Psycho Starship Rampage est un roguelike décliné sous la forme d’un shoot them up horizontal et développé par un petit studio français. 

Deux modes de jeu nous sont proposés :
Le mode campagne tout d’abord nous permet de naviguer sur une carte galactique dont le principe est très similaire à FTL. En effet notre vaisseau est poursuivi par une flotte ennemie et notre but est d’atteindre le bout de la carte (la terre) avant que celle-ci ne nous rattrape.
On se déplace donc dans ce but de nœud en nœud sur la carte, chaque nœud représentant un niveau à nettoyer et contenant sont lots d’ennemis et d’équipement à ramasser. En cas de défaite dans le niveau on ne bouge pas permettant à la flotte ennemie de nous rattraper.
Les choix pour parvenir à la victoire sont donc multiples et les résultats toujours incertains. Aller vous tenter un chemin long pour amasser le plus d’équipements possible au risque de vous faire rattraper par l’ennemi ? Ou plutôt un chemin court quitte à se retrouver désarmé face aux redoutables derniers niveaux ?

Le mode survie quant à lui est une succession de niveaux aléatoires entre lesquels on peut améliorer sont vaisseau grâce aux équipements récoltés. Tous les équipements ne sont pas disponible au début et ceux-ci se débloque en accomplissant certains objectifs (Détruire 1000 ennemis avec un canon laser par exemple).

La personnalisation du vaisseau accessible dans les deux modes de jeu est clairement le point fort du titre celle-ci laissant totalement libre court à l’imagination du joueur. Les possibilités sont conséquente grâce notamment à un nombre varié d’équipements (canons à plasma, torpilles, boucliers, moteurs, générateurs…). Chaque équipement aillant par ailleurs des statistiques uniques.

Niveau direction artistique le jeu s’en tire très bien. Les arrière-plans des niveaux sont très jolis et le design « néon » des vaisseaux bien que simpliste est très agréable et se marie parfaitement à la musique électronique soignée du titre. Les bruitages sont corrects et le tout offre un rendu convainquant.

[h1]Points positifs : [/h1]
[list]
[*]Durée de vie quasi illimitée grâce à la génération aléatoire des niveaux
[*]Liberté complète du joueur au niveau de la construction de son vaisseau
[*]Musique excellente
[*]Graphisme agréable
[*]Support complet de la manette
[*]Multijoueur coopératif local (jusqu’à 4 joueur)
[/list]

[h1]Points négatifs : [/h1]
[list]
[*]L’interface de personalisation du vaisseau n’est pas très intuitive (heureusement un petit tutorial est présent et on s’y fait vite)
[/list]
